title: Relative motion
examples: What is the fastest way to cross a river?
How does the current affect my speed?
If I swim at a certain speed, what is my actual speed across?

explain.say: Today we learn about relative velocity. This means speed compared to something else. We look at how motion changes depending on the observer.
Consider a boat moving in a river. The boat's speed is relative to the water. The water's speed is relative to the bank.
To find the boat's speed relative to the bank, we add the two speeds. This is the principle of velocity addition. The resultant velocity is the sum.
For a river crossing, if you aim straight across, the current pushes you downstream. The resultant path is diagonal. We use Pythagoras for the actual speed.

For example, if you swim at five meters per second across and the river flows at three meters per second, your actual speed is found using Pythagoras. The actual speed is the square root of five squared plus three squared. This gives you a speed of five point eight three meters per second.

faq.q: Do I always add the speeds together?
faq.a: No, you only add them if the two motions are perfectly aligned in the same direction. If they are perpendicular, you must use Pythagoras.

faq.q: Does the angle matter in river problems?
faq.a: Yes, the angle determines the direction of the resultant velocity. If you aim at an angle, the current will change your path.
asks: How do I account for angles?

faq.q: If I want to land directly across, what should I do?
faq.a: You must aim upstream at an angle to counteract the river's current. This makes your resultant path point straight across the river.
asks: How do I go straight across?
What angle should I aim at?

faq.q: Is the speed relative to the water the same as relative to the bank?
faq.a: No, they are different. The speed relative to the water is what your engine or muscles provide. The speed relative to the bank includes the water's push.
asks: Which speed do I use for calculation?
What is the difference between the two speeds?

faq.q: Does the time taken change if I aim at an angle?
faq.a: The time taken to cross depends only on the component of velocity perpendicular to the flow. Angling changes the path but not the crossing time if the perpendicular speed is constant.

facts: Velocity is a vector quantity, meaning it has both magnitude and direction.
Relative velocity is the velocity of an object measured with respect to a moving frame of reference.
When two velocities are perpendicular, the resultant speed is found using the Pythagorean theorem.
The time taken to cross a river depends only on the component of velocity perpendicular to the flow.

quiz.say: A swimmer swims at eight meters per second perpendicular to a river current flowing at three meters per second. What is the actual speed of the swimmer relative to the bank?
quiz.why: The perpendicular and current velocities are at right angles, so we use Pythagoras to find the resultant speed.

wrong.0: This mistake happens if the student forgets to use the current speed at all.
wrong.1: This occurs if the student incorrectly squares and adds the speeds without taking the square root.
wrong.3: This is a common error because students incorrectly add the two speeds together.

quiz.say: A boat aims upstream at 10 meters per second, while the river flows at 4 meters per second. What is the boat's resultant speed relative to the bank?
quiz.why: Since the boat aims directly against the current, the speeds are in opposite directions, so we subtract the smaller from the larger.

wrong.1: This mistake happens if the student incorrectly adds the two speeds together.
wrong.2: This is incorrect because it suggests multiplying the speeds together.
wrong.3: This might happen if the student subtracts the smaller speed from the larger speed twice.

quiz.say: If a swimmer aims at an angle to land straight across a river, what must the angle compensate for?
quiz.why: To counteract the sideways push of the current, the swimmer must aim upstream at an angle to cancel out that sideways drift.

wrong.1: The swimmer's own speed is what they are trying to maintain, not what they need to compensate for.
wrong.2: The distance is the outcome, not the force or velocity that needs balancing.
wrong.3: The engine power is a factor, but the required compensation is specifically against the water's flow.
